Hazar-gaddah
hay-zar-GAD-uh
proper noun
Hebrew Chatsar Gaddah, “the village of Gad” or “court of fortune” — a settlement in the far south (the Negeb) of Judah, near the coast of Edom.

📖 Biblical Definition

Hazar-gaddah was one of the uttermost cities of the tribe of Judah toward the coast of Edom southward, named in the great catalogue of the inheritance: “And Hazargaddah, and Heshmon, and Bethpalet” (Josh 15:27). It is a name that appears once and then falls silent, a mere dot in the dry country of the south. Yet its silence preaches. When Joshua divided the land by lot, the LORD did not overlook the least and dustiest hamlet on the edge of the wilderness; every village was numbered, allotted, and recorded, for “the land shall be divided by lot: according to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit” (Num 26:55). The very meaning of the name, a “court of fortune,” is redeemed in Israel’s theology: what the heathen ascribe to blind fortune, the covenant people ascribe to the sovereign hand that setteth the bounds of the peoples. Hazar-gaddah stands as a small witness that not one good thing the LORD promised failed; the whole land, to its farthest village, came into the hand of His people, that they might dwell in it and serve Him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

An obscure village in the far south of Judah toward Edom (Josh 15:27); a witness that God allotted every least town of the inheritance and forgot none.

expand to see more

HAZAR-GADDAH, a village in the Negeb of Judah, near the border of Edom.

Named once, among the uttermost cities of Judah’s inheritance (Josh 15:27).

The name means “court of fortune” — redeemed in Israel to the LORD’s providence.

Every village was allotted by lot, not one overlooked (Num 26:55).

A small witness that God’s promise of the land failed in nothing (Josh 21:45).

📖 Key Scripture

Josh 15:27 — "And Hazargaddah, and Heshmon, and Bethpalet,"

Num 26:55 — "Notwithstanding the land shall be divided by lot: according to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit."

Josh 21:45 — "There failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass."

Deu 32:8 — "When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

An obscure town of the south; it recovers the doctrine that God’s providence, not fortune, allots every bound of habitation, down to the least village.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The name “court of fortune” might tempt the reader to think Israel shared the pagan worship of luck and chance. She did not. The lot was cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof was of the LORD. What the nations round about called Gad, fortune, and set a table for, Israel confessed to be the appointed portion of a faithful God.

The principle to recover is that God determines the bounds of every people’s habitation. He “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26). There is no fortune, no blind chance, no roll of the dice outside His decree; the smallest village in the driest corner of the south was given by the same hand that upholds the stars.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

An obscure village in the far south of Judah toward Edom; a witness that God allotted every least town and forgot none.

expand to see more

Hazar-gaddah — “court of fortune,” a village of southern Judah (Josh 15:27).

One of the uttermost cities toward the coast of Edom.

The name’s “fortune” is redeemed to the LORD’s providence.

The land was divided by lot, yet wholly disposed of God (Num 26:55).

Not one good thing the LORD promised failed (Josh 21:45).

Usage

"Hazar-gaddah lay among the uttermost cities of Judah toward Edom."

"The village was allotted by lot, yet given by the hand of God."

"Its name, a court of fortune, was redeemed to confess divine providence."
